title: Checkpoint: Justice and the Good Society
objective: After this level you can compare the reasons thinkers give for who should rule, how free people should be and what makes a society just.
summary: This chapter’s thinkers disagree about who should rule, how free people should be and what a fair share is, and each view meets a named critic.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: who should rule, how free, and who gets what?
cards.body: Every thinker in this chapter answered at least one of these three questions, and each answer met a named critic. Line them up.

items.label: Who should rule?
points: Plato: philosophers, trained to know the Good
Confucius: virtue and ritual teach shame

items.label: How free?
points: Mill: free unless you harm others
Devlin: law may defend shared morality

items.label: What is fair?
points: Rawls: rules chosen behind a veil of ignorance

cards.headline: Two ways to judge a fair share
cards.body: Rawls and Nozick look at different things. Rawls’s difference principle judges a distribution by how its worst-off position fares. Nozick’s entitlement theory judges holdings by their history: were they justly acquired or freely transferred? The same unequal result can pass one test and fail the other.

cards.headline: Rulers or rules?
cards.body: Plato wanted rulers who know the Good. Han Fei doubted such rulers would come along: most are mediocre, so build a government of laws that works anyway. One trusts the best person; the other plans for the average one.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: What makes a society just for Plato, Rawls and Nozick, and why they disagree.
Why Confucians trusted virtuous rulers while Legalists like Han Fei trusted laws.
How Mill’s harm principle limits power, and why Devlin thought law may defend morality.
Why Wollstonecraft and Beauvoir blamed women’s situation on upbringing, not nature.

questions.prompt: Justice and the Good Society recap: what does Mill say is the only purpose for which power may rightfully be used over someone against their will?

options.label: To prevent harm to others
To enforce shared morality
To improve the person’s own health
options.rationale: Mill says their own good isn’t enough.

options.label: To keep the ruler in power

questions.explanation: Mill’s harm principle: power may be used over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others.

questions.prompt: Justice and the Good Society recap: in his 1844 Manuscripts, what did Marx call the condition of workers cut off from their product, work, others and nature?

options.label: Bad faith
Immanence
Alienation
Exploitation
options.rationale: That’s Marx’s separate charge about value.

questions.explanation: Marx named four dimensions of alienated labour.

questions.prompt: In Justice and the Good Society, why can the same unequal result pass Nozick’s test but fail Rawls’s?

options.label: Nozick checks equality; Rawls checks history
Both check only the total amount of wealth
options.rationale: Neither test is about the total.

options.label: Rawls rejects every inequality; Nozick allows some
options.rationale: Rawls allows inequalities that help the least advantaged.

options.label: Nozick checks its history; Rawls checks how the worst-off fare

questions.explanation: Nozick asks how holdings came about; Rawls asks how the least advantaged position fares.

questions.prompt: In Justice and the Good Society, why did Han Fei, unlike Plato, refuse to build government around the best possible ruler?

options.label: Sage rulers are rare and most are mediocre
He thought the best ruler would become a tyrant
options.rationale: His worry was rarity, not tyranny.

options.label: He wanted philosophers to run the courts instead
He believed rulers should be chosen by lot

questions.explanation: Most rulers are mediocre, so Han Fei wanted a system of laws that works under ordinary rulers.

questions.prompt: Justice and the Good Society recap: which critic argued that Beauvoir generalized from white, middle-class women’s lives?

options.label: Mary Wollstonecraft
options.rationale: She wrote in 1792, long before Beauvoir.

options.label: Elizabeth Spelman
Leo Strauss
Patrick Devlin

questions.explanation: Elizabeth Spelman (1988) argued that feminist philosophers, Beauvoir among them, ignored race, class and culture.
